Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Media / News: Related news, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Marisol is a 70-year-old Colombian-American woman who has worked as a fashion designer for nearly four decades, building a modest but respected atelier in Miami that specializes in bridal and quinceañera wear. She has been married for forty-one years and describes her husband as her closest companion. She was referred for psychological assessment following a conversation with her primary care physician, to whom she had finally disclosed that she had not slept through the night in over two years.

The event that fractured Marisol's sense of safety occurred during a family visit to her hometown in Colombia, where she had traveled with her younger sister, Claudia, to attend a cousin's wedding. On the second day of the visit, the two women were walking through a crowded outdoor market in the early afternoon heat when a confrontation erupted between two groups of men nearby. Within seconds, the situation escalated beyond anything Marisol could have anticipated. Claudia, who had stepped slightly ahead to look at a textile stall, was caught in the violence. Marisol watched from fewer than ten feet away, frozen, as her sister collapsed. By the time she reached her, it was already too late. Claudia died before an ambulance arrived. No one was ever charged. The men responsible dispersed into the crowd and, as far as Marisol has been able to determine, have faced no legal consequence whatsoever.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol returned to Miami and attempted to resume her work. The atelier's studio is open-air in the warmer months, and Miami's climate means that the dense, pressing heat of midday is a near-daily reality. What she did not anticipate was that the specific quality of warmth on her forearms — the same temperature she felt standing in that market — could, without any warning, collapse the distance between then and now entirely. She has described moments at her cutting table when the air shifts and the memory does not simply return but arrives whole, immersive, and completely real: the sounds of the market, the smell of the fabric stalls, the sight of Claudia falling. These episodes leave her gripping the edge of her worktable, disoriented, certain for a moment that she is still there. Because of this, she has gradually moved more of her work indoors and has asked her assistant to handle client fittings during the hottest hours of the day, offering scheduling explanations that have nothing to do with the real reason.

She had come to believe, with quiet but unyielding conviction, that she was responsible for what happened. She had been the one to suggest that particular market. She had agreed when Claudia said she wanted to walk ahead. In Marisol's accounting of that afternoon, there were a dozen moments at which a different choice on her part might have changed everything, and she has returned to each of them countless times. Alongside this sits a related belief she has never spoken aloud until recently: that her presence, her decisions, her failure to act in those first seconds constituted a kind of abandonment of the person she most loved.

She no longer watches television news or reads online media. When her husband turns on a broadcast that touches on violence in Latin America, she leaves the room without explaining why. She has stopped attending the annual memorial Mass her family holds for Claudia, telling relatives she is unwell, because the gathering brings her sister's absence into the room in a way that feels unbearable. More quietly, she has noticed that when something genuinely good happens — a daughter's promotion, a successful collection, an anniversary dinner — she finds herself pulling back from the warmth of it, as though allowing herself to feel happiness is a form of exposure she cannot afford. What frightened her most was not the grief itself but the sense that she had no control over when any of it would arrive, and that the world had confirmed, through Claudia's death and the absence of any justice, that safety was simply not something she could rely on.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when she was fitting a young bride and found herself unable to speak for nearly a minute, standing in her own studio in broad daylight, somewhere else entirely. She came to the intake appointment hoping, she said quietly, to be able to attend her granddaughter's quinceañera in the spring without leaving early.
